name: Brain-lung-thyroid syndrome
aliases: benign hereditary chorea with lung and thyroid disease

clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations or deletions of NKX2-1 (also known as TTF-1)
Classically affects three organ systems: the brain, the lungs and the thyroid, in variable combination
Neurological features include benign hereditary chorea and, in infancy, hypotonia and delayed motor milestones
Respiratory involvement ranges from neonatal respiratory distress to recurrent infections and interstitial lung disease
Thyroid disease spans congenital hypothyroidism to compensated or subclinical dysfunction
Not all three systems are involved in every patient, so partial phenotypes are common
Diagnosis is confirmed genetically; the combination of chorea, lung disease and thyroid dysfunction is a strong clue
reference.pathophysiology: NKX2-1 encodes a transcription factor essential for development and function of the brain (notably the basal ganglia), lung and thyroid. Haploinsufficiency from a mutation or deletion of one allele disrupts gene programmes in these three organs, producing the characteristic triad. In the lung, NKX2-1 regulates surfactant protein genes, linking the disorder to the surfactant dysfunction spectrum. The variable involvement and severity reflect the differing dose sensitivity of each organ to reduced transcription-factor activity.
additionalDifferentials: Cerebral palsy with a movement disorder
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing for NKX2-1 mutations or deletions
Thyroid function tests and thyroid imaging
Chest imaging and, where indicated, assessment for interstitial lung disease
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory distress with associated hypotonia
reference.prognosis: The prognosis depends on the severity of lung involvement; chorea is typically non-progressive and thyroid dysfunction is treatable, so many patients do well, though severe respiratory disease worsens the outlook.
pitfalls: Diagnosing isolated benign hereditary chorea and missing associated lung or thyroid disease
Overlooking subtle or compensated thyroid dysfunction
Not considering the syndrome in unexplained neonatal respiratory distress with hypotonia
Assuming all three organ systems must be involved to make the diagnosis
management: Levothyroxine replacement for congenital, compensated or subclinical hypothyroidism
Symptomatic treatment of disabling benign hereditary chorea, for example with tetrabenazine or a trial of levodopa
Respiratory support for neonatal respiratory distress, recurrent infections and interstitial lung disease
Developmental support with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy for hypotonia and motor delay
Surveillance of thyroid function, respiratory status and neurological progression
Multidisciplinary coordination across neurology, respiratory medicine, endocrinology and clinical genetics
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant NKX2-1 inheritance with family testing
